details:
ClimateTrend Saudi is an interactive climate-analysis tool created by Team AstroQuant Saudi. We wanted to explore a simple but important question: Are temperature and rainfall patterns changing in Saudi Arabian cities, and how confidently can we identify those changes?

Using NASA POWER data from 2001 to 2025, we developed an R Shiny dashboard that compares Riyadh, Jeddah, and Abha. Users can select a city and climate variable, explore historical graphs, and examine estimated trends, confidence intervals, and statistical significance.

Our goal is to make Earth science data easier for students, researchers, and the public to understand, while encouraging careful interpretation of scientific evidence.

The idea behind our project

Saudi Arabia has cities with very different climates. Riyadh has a hot desert environment, Jeddah is a coastal city, and Abha has a higher-elevation climate. We chose these three cities because comparing their environmental patterns can help us understand how climate trends differ across locations.

Instead of simply showing weather graphs, we wanted to build a tool that helps users investigate environmental changes scientifically.

How our solution works

Our project uses historical NASA POWER temperature and precipitation datasets covering 2001–2025.

We process these data using R, calculate annual temperature averages and precipitation totals, and use statistical methods to estimate trends over time.

Our analysis includes linear regression, changes per decade, 95% confidence intervals, and adjusted p-values. These methods help us assess whether an observed trend is supported by statistical evidence.

We developed an interactive application using R Shiny. Users can select Riyadh, Jeddah, or Abha, choose temperature or precipitation, and explore the corresponding graphs and statistical findings.

What we discovered

Our preliminary analysis estimated an increasing temperature trend for Riyadh of approximately 0.288°C per decade, with a 95% confidence interval from 0.091°C to 0.485°C per decade.

The exploratory results also suggested differences in temperature and precipitation trends among the three cities.

We recognize that these estimates come from NASA-derived meteorological data, and that statistical significance does not establish the causes of environmental change. Further validation is required before drawing stronger conclusions.

What makes our project useful

ClimateTrend Saudi brings climate data, statistical analysis, and interactive visualization into one accessible platform.

It encourages users to look beyond whether a graph rises or falls and ask how large a change is, how uncertain the estimate may be, and whether the finding is statistically supported.

The project was designed to be practical for university students using freely available data and open-source software.

Future development

We hope to expand the platform to additional Saudi cities, introduce more Earth science variables, and incorporate further statistical validation methods. Our longer-term goal is to make climate information easier to explore, understand, and use in education and environmental research.
